title: FDA uses AI to choose where to concentrate food inspections; an imported-seafood pilot ran for years
summary: FDA reports that its imported-seafood model recommended samples at 328 U.S. ports and that its Elsa tool helped find inspection targets, with no figure on hazards found or illnesses prevented.
account: FDA's update of 22 August 2022 states that its operational imported-seafood model returned sampling recommendations to reviewers at all 328 U.S. ports of entry from February through July 2021. The update says that the pilot proved successful and that the real-time model returned a sample recommendation within seconds. It gives no figure for hazards found. Civil Eats reported on 27 May 2025 that FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, appearing before a Senate committee the previous week, said that the agency was using AI to identify where to concentrate food inspections and that AI can sometimes find patterns faster than people. He added that a human reviews the information. The article notes that FDA had been working for several years on a pilot focused on imported seafood. It also notes that FDA had announced an agency-wide generative AI rollout, and an FDA spokesperson said that all centers would run on a unified platform by 30 June. A 2 June update to the article records the launch of Elsa, FDA's generative AI tool, said to be used in part to identify high-priority inspection targets. Jaydee Hanson of the Center for Food Safety is quoted on the risks of using AI amid staff cuts. FDA's announcement of 2 June 2025 describes Elsa as a large language model tool in a secure GovCloud environment, separate from the seafood model, and says that the agency is already using it to identify high-priority inspection targets. CNN reported on 23 July 2025 that FDA staff said that Elsa makes up studies. Makary told CNN that most FDA scientists used it to find studies and summarize meetings. No source gives a numerical improvement in detection or health outcomes, and no inspection outcome, detection or recall is attributed to the AI.
purpose: Prioritize food inspection targets, including imported seafood, using pattern recognition over agency data.

fields.headline: FDA uses AI to target food inspections

value.role: SHA-256 of the complete public record and its assessments

provenance.basis: SHA-256 of the public record, its assessments, and its displayed answers and notes, excluding its own identifier and the derived coverage summary.

fields.account: FDA's update of 22 August 2022 states that its operational imported-seafood model returned sampling recommendations to reviewers at all 328 U.S. ports of entry from February through July 2021. The update says that the pilot proved successful and that the real-time model returned a sample recommendation within seconds. It gives no figure for hazards found. Civil Eats reported on 27 May 2025 that FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, appearing before a Senate committee the previous week, said that the agency was using AI to identify where to concentrate food inspections and that AI can sometimes find patterns faster than people. He added that a human reviews the information. The article notes that FDA had been working for several years on a pilot focused on imported seafood. It also notes that FDA had announced an agency-wide generative AI rollout, and an FDA spokesperson said that all centers would run on a unified platform by 30 June. A 2 June update to the article records the launch of Elsa, FDA's generative AI tool, said to be used in part to identify high-priority inspection targets. Jaydee Hanson of the Center for Food Safety is quoted on the risks of using AI amid staff cuts. FDA's announcement of 2 June 2025 describes Elsa as a large language model tool in a secure GovCloud environment, separate from the seafood model, and says that the agency is already using it to identify high-priority inspection targets. CNN reported on 23 July 2025 that FDA staff said that Elsa makes up studies. Makary told CNN that most FDA scientists used it to find studies and summarize meetings. No source gives a numerical improvement in detection or health outcomes, and no inspection outcome, detection or recall is attributed to the AI.

produced_by: An agency-wide generative AI rollout announced in May 2025
must_hold: Human review of AI outputs, as the Commissioner stated
